doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Alan Thicke, the Orlando special and the Different Strokes session
summary: A prerecorded guitar feature for Tony Orlando's NBC special led to a call for a rapid Different Strokes pilot recording.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: How funny. Anything on your little list that I didn’t ask you about?

No I think we did pretty good. I do have — back to the recording thing, with Tony Orlando we did a TV show called “Tony Orlando’s First Special.” It was for NBC. And the director was Alan Thicke. And so we did the show and I had a feature, a guitar feature. Well anyway, longer story, it was kind of a Spanish type thing on the song “Up on the Roof,” all right, and they had dancers and all this stuff they were going to do. So we did a pre-record in the studio and again I’m doing all these fancy jamming things over this one section. And they decided they were going to use that track. And I said okay, that’s fine. And then they’d say “oh by the way, be there early, you’ll be in make-up, you’ve got to be in make-up. Well yeah, they’re going to put this van on this rooftop set and you’ll be playing your instruments.” And I thought good, we just spent a couple of hours in the studio messing around and I’m improvising Spanish type licks all over this piece and I’m going to be there with my guitar, am I going to look like an idiot like playing something that’s not in sync with the music? So I asked the director, or the engineer rather, can you give me a quick cassette of what we just did?” “Oh sure.” So he made me a cassette of it, and then I took it back to the hotel room and I practiced with the cassette, trying to remember what I did, and memorize my finger patterns. So this was wonderful. So then when it came time for the shoot I mentioned to somebody, I’ve got my solo memorized, so if you need to get anywhere near my hands I’ll be right. Well this guy went running to the director and told him. And the director made an announcement that I was in sync with the music. Ah, this is great. So out comes Tony Orlando with his costume, and he says “you want to hear something great? My guitar player spent all night learning his solo so that he would be in sync for the camera. Isn’t that dedication?” I’d © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -22-

been on the gig for about two weeks. So the other guys in the band they’re looking at me like you apple polisher. Not why I did it. I just wanted to make sure that if I was down here and the music was up here that the guys at home wouldn’t look at me and say “you didn’t play that” or whatever. But anyway so I did that, and that came off okay. But then I went home to Utica, and about two days later Alan Thicke called up our musical director, Reg Powell, and said look, Norman Lear is going to be doing a show, he’s got a pilot, and it’s called “Different Strokes.” And we need a band to come in quick and cut this thing. Now you guys just did the show and you’re very good, do you think you could get together and come in later on this afternoon and do this show? And he said “let me see call everybody and see if I can find them.” Now meanwhile I’m in Utica, and the other guys all live in LA. So they were able to go in and do the “Different Strokes” theme song and they said well it’s on spec. We don’t know if the network is going to pick it up or whatever. So we can either pay you for the session, or you can do it for free and we’ll put you on speculation. And they said “well what’s the deal on spec?” “Well every 13 weeks you get scale, and then each day that it’s played out of that 13 weeks, you get scale per day.” And so it’s every 13 weeks full session, plus a daily rate on those kind of things. Now naturally I’m in Utica so I don’t get to be part of this thing. All right? So obviously the show got picked up, “Different Strokes” ran for what, ten years or whatever the thing was, and these guys got residual checks every 13 weeks the show ran, plus new use, plus overseas, I mean they’re probably still getting checks. It came out to some nice money. But you had to be in Los Angeles. That’s part of the thing, it’s something else for people that want to be a career musician, now it’s different with the Internet, but for situations like that, you’ve got to be where it was happening.
